1377-79. οἷος δ’ οὐρανόθεν πυρόεις ἀναπάλλεται: it is also written ἀπολάμπεται. He speaks about the stars that dart across and quickly disappear, which by the swiftness of their motion have something similar to one rushing upon [something]. He calls ὁλκός the light that is dragged along with it by its swiftness. Such appearances Musaeus (2 B 17 Diels-Kranz) says rise from the ocean and are extinguished in the aether. Apollonius plausibly called the stars mentioned by Musaeus 'flashes'; for the gleams that occur, imperceptible because of their swiftness, are called 'flashes' from some source. But it is implausible to compare Jason, as he goes to a dangerous contest, to such a star, which is extinguished immediately upon appearing. But if someone should say that he has likened him to Pyroeis, about whom Epigenes in his work On the Chaldean Mathematics, after first speaking about the planets, of which he says one is Pyroeis, called by the Greeks Ares, but by the Chaldeans Heracles 〈...〉; for he says that as it moves along, flashes and sparks occur, but Pyroeis is slow-moving.
